strengths: The core insight — that a fixed token order imposes a restrictive inductive bias on AR generative classifiers, and that marginalizing over token orders yields more comprehensive predictions — is clearly motivated and empirically substantiated (Fig. 1, per-token analyses in Figs. 3–5, Table 1).

The proposed order-marginalized classifier is technically sound: the Jensen lower bound (Eq. 5) is a reasonable and practically validated choice over direct Monte Carlo likelihood estimation, and this design decision is properly ablated (Table 5) and connected to the analogous observation for diffusion classifiers (training objective vs. true ELBO).

Comprehensive and fair experimental evaluation: comparisons against discriminative (ViT, DINOv2, ResNets), diffusion (DiT, SiT, REPA variants), joint energy-based (DAT), and AR (LlamaGen, VAR, A-VARC) baselines with matched model sizes, resolution, and token counts; diffusion baselines are strengthened via careful ELBO weighting ablations (Appendix D).

Strong and consistent results: new state-of-the-art among generative classifiers on ImageNet and OOD benchmarks (Table 2), clear accuracy–efficiency advantage over diffusion classifiers (up to 25× faster, Fig. 6), and convincing WILDS results (Table 6) showing robustness to subpopulation and distribution shifts.

Thoughtful analyses beyond headline numbers: per-token discriminative likelihoods, prefix-length effects, tokenizer robustness study with a motivated latent-noise augmentation (Tables 3–4), error analysis vs. DINOv2 (Fig. 7), and evidence that DM-side noise averaging brings no gains (Appendix C).

Good reproducibility posture: training details for reproduced models are provided in Appendix A, code and models are promised for release, and evaluation subsets/fairness concerns (2K subsets, DiT/SiT weighting) are addressed transparently.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: the contribution is largely an insightful application/combination of an existing any-order AR model (RandAR) with the established diffusion-classifier evaluation methodology (Bayes rule with weighted/averaged likelihoods); the main technical addition is the Jensen lower-bound aggregation, which is simple, and the work could be viewed as an empirical study rather than a new algorithmic framework.

Statistical rigor of the results is limited: main ImageNet results are computed on 2K-image subsets without error bars, confidence intervals, or variance across random order seeds; given that some margins (e.g., RandAR-XL 0.813 vs. 0.815 at K=4) and baseline gaps could be sensitive to sampling, some significance quantification would strengthen the claims.

Absolute efficiency remains a practical limitation: even at K=20, the method requires M×K forward passes (M classes, hundreds to thousands of sequences per image), so the celebrated competitiveness with DINOv2 comes at a large inference cost relative to discriminative models; the paper acknowledges this but the scalability story beyond 1000 classes is untested.

The comparison with DINOv2 involves models trained with substantially different data regimes and pretraining setups (DINOv2 retrained on ImageNet-1K here, but architecture/backbone differences, e.g., DAT using ConvNeXt-L, complicate strict like-for-like conclusions); also IN-A remains a clear weakness (0.233 vs. 0.345), which is somewhat downplayed.

Some analysis is more suggestive than conclusive: the explanations for the prefix-length peak (Fig. 5), for why the lower bound outperforms direct likelihood estimation, and for why noise averaging does not help DMs are hypotheses without direct experimental verification.
The WILDS evaluation, while valuable, uses a somewhat narrow baseline set (ERM, RWY, sigma-stitching, DiT) and small models; comparisons against stronger modern robustness/SSL methods are absent.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core insight: fixed token ordering in AR models imposes a restrictive inductive bias for classification, and marginalizing over multiple token orders yields more comprehensive predictive signal. The motivating example (Fig. 1) and per-token analyses (Figs. 3-5) make this observation concrete and interpretable.

Strong empirical results: order-marginalized RandAR classifiers establish a new state of the art among generative classifiers, clearly outperforming diffusion classifiers (DiT, SiT, REPA variants, A-VARC) on ImageNet and OOD benchmarks, while being up to 25x faster in inference. The efficiency-accuracy trade-off analysis (Fig. 6, Table 7) is convincing.

First work to benchmark generative classifiers against state-of-the-art self-supervised discriminative models (DINOv2), showing competitive OOD robustness; this comparison is valuable for the community and raises the bar for GC evaluations.

Unusually thorough fairness controls: diffusion baselines were retrained/reproduced with ablations over ELBO weighting schemes (Table 8), v-prediction vs epsilon-prediction, noise-sample averaging (Appendix C), and tokenizer ablations including a thoughtful latent-noise augmentation analysis (Tables 3-4).

Broad experimental scope beyond ImageNet: WILDS benchmarks (Camelyon17, CelebA, FMoW) demonstrate robustness to real-world subpopulation and distribution shifts, strengthening the generality of the claims.

The likelihood estimation ablation (lower bound via Jensen's inequality vs. direct Monte Carlo estimate, Table 5) is a non-obvious and useful finding, well-aligned with the training objective argument.
Code and models promised to be released; baselines reproduced strictly following official implementations, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is modest: the classifier is essentially Monte Carlo averaging of order-conditional likelihoods from an existing pretrained RandAR model (Eq. 5), a fairly direct application of an existing any-order AR model to the established Bayes-rule generative classification recipe. The scientific contribution rests mainly on the analysis and empirical findings rather than a new algorithm.

The proposed method introduces a new tunable hyperparameter K (number of sampled orders) whose selection could implicitly tune on the evaluation sets; the paper states results use 'sufficiently large K for near-optimal performance' rather than a fixed budget, which slightly weakens the efficiency comparison fairness.

Main ImageNet results are reported on 2K subsets of IN-Val/IN-S/IN-C (following prior protocol); while the authors verified subset-size stability, exact numbers carry nontrivial variance and no error bars or seed variance are reported anywhere.

Compute cost scales linearly with the number of classes (M x K forward passes per image); while cheaper than diffusion classifiers, this remains a practical limitation for large label spaces, and the discussion of mitigation (e.g., distillation) is deferred entirely to future work.

Several presentation issues: broken LaTeX in Equations 1-3, a misdirected cross-reference (noise augmentation ablation is discussed in Sec. 6.4 but cited as 6.5), and a placeholder for the code URL in the abstract. These do not affect the science but indicate insufficient polish.

The hypothesis explaining why the Jensen lower bound outperforms the true likelihood estimate (alignment with the training objective) is plausible but not rigorously validated; the DM noise-averaging explanation in Appendix C is similarly speculative.

Comparison with DINOv2 is somewhat asymmetric: DINOv2 is adapted/retrained on ImageNet1K for this paper, while much of DINOv2's known strength comes from larger-scale pretraining; the paper acknowledges the in-domain gap but this framing could be more explicit.

The raster-order vs. random-order K=1 gap (Table 1) shows the random-order model is worse per single order, meaning the approach depends on the availability of a specifically designed any-order model (RandAR); generalization to other AR architectures is untested.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: the paper identifies a genuine limitation of prior AR-based generative classifiers (fixed raster-scan token order) and connects it to the coarse-to-fine behavior of diffusion models, providing a conceptual framing (DMs as implicit spectral AR models) that is insightful.

The proposed order-marginalized classification scheme is simple, technically sound, and effective: using RandAR's position-conditioned any-order likelihoods and averaging log-likelihoods over K sampled orders (Jensen lower bound) yields consistent gains over raster-order AR classifiers (e.g., 0.701 -> 0.780 on IN-Val for L/16, 0.813 for XL/16).

Comprehensive and fair experimental design: baselines span discriminative (supervised ViT, DINOv2), diffusion (DiT, SiT, SiT+REPA, with careful weighting-scheme ablations to strengthen the DM baselines), joint energy-based (DAT), and AR (LlamaGen, VAR, A-VARC) families, with matched architectures, resolution, and token counts. Reproducing weaker baselines from scratch rather than using stale checkpoints is commendable.

Notable empirical milestone: the method reportedly achieves SOTA among generative classifiers and is the first GC to be competitive with a strong SSL model (DINOv2), surpassing it on 3 of 5 OOD benchmarks — a meaningful result for the generative-classification research direction.

Strong analysis sections: per-token discriminative likelihood maps, per-token accuracy vs. prefix length, prefix ablations (Appendix B), likelihood-estimation strategy ablation (Table 5), tokenizer robustness study with a novel latent noise augmentation (Section 6.4, Table 4), DM noise-averaging control (Appendix C), WILDS robustness experiments, and qualitative error analysis. Together these give unusually thorough support for the claims.
Efficiency results are convincing: up to 25x faster inference than diffusion classifiers at better accuracy, with runtime measurements on a single A100 across multiple operating points (Fig. 6).

Code and models are promised to be released, and training details in Appendix A are sufficiently complete for reproducibility. Limitations and future directions (self-supervised AR training, adaptive order prediction, distillation) are thoughtfully discussed.
weaknesses: Dependence on a single any-order architecture: all conclusions about order marginalization rest on RandAR; it remains unverified whether the gains generalize to other any-order or masked-token models (e.g., MaskGIT-style parallel decoding trained with random orders), which weakens the breadth of the central claim.

The Jensen lower-bound estimator (Eq. 5) is used instead of the true order-marginalized likelihood; the justification is largely empirical ('RandAR was trained on Equation 5'). A tighter theoretical or more rigorous treatment of why the lower bound is better aligned would strengthen the contribution, since the two estimators diverge as K grows.

Evaluation protocol limitations: main ImageNet results are computed on 2K subsets of IN-Val/IN-S/IN-C (following [33]). Although the authors verified stability, full-set evaluation would make headline numbers (e.g., 0.813 IN-Val) more directly comparable to the literature.

Practical scaling concerns: inference requires M x K forward passes per image (20 x 1000 for IN-Val), and even at 25x speedup the absolute cost (~20s/image for XL per Fig. 6) is far from practical; the paper is honest about this but the immediate applicability is limited.

The latent noise augmentation is a nontrivial training modification specific to the LlamaGen tokenizer; its interaction with the order-marginalization effect (i.e., how much of the improvement over LlamaGen/VAR baselines is attributable to ordering vs. augmentation) is only partially disentangled.

IN-A performance (0.233 XL) remains notably weaker than DINOv2 (0.345); the paper acknowledges this but does not analyze the cause (e.g., tokenizer brittleness vs. model bias), which would have been informative.

Missing significance testing / variance estimates for the key comparisons (only WILDS experiments average 3 seeds); several reported margins (e.g., over DiT-XL on IN-C JPEG) are small enough that uncertainty matters.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core insight: token ordering imposes a restrictive inductive bias on AR-based generative classifiers, and marginalizing over multiple orders via any-order AR models (RandAR) yields substantially better classification. The Jensen lower-bound estimator (Eq. 5) is simple, principled, and empirically far more effective than direct Monte Carlo log-likelihood estimation.

Comprehensive empirical evidence: comparisons across discriminative (ViT, DINOv2), diffusion (DiT, SiT, REPA, MeanFlow), joint (DAT), and AR (LlamaGen, VAR, A-VARC+) baselines at matched architecture, resolution, and token count; evaluation on ImageNet-Val plus multiple OOD benchmarks (IN-R/S/A/C) and real-world distribution shifts (WILDS: Camelylon17, CelebA, FMoW).

Strong headline results: state-of-the-art among generative classifiers, competitive with DINOv2 on OOD benchmarks, and up to 25x faster inference than diffusion classifiers — a meaningful practical advantage given the well-known computational cost of diffusion classifiers.

Thorough analysis and ablations: per-token discriminative likelihoods and accuracy visualizations, prefix-length analysis, likelihood-estimation strategy ablation, tokenizer robustness study (MaskGIT vs LlamaGen) with a useful latent-noise augmentation, generalization to RAR-B (beyond RandAR), and a theoretically grounded equivalence between the AO-AR objective and the masked-diffusion ELBO (Appendix D) with supporting experiments (Sec. 6.7).

Good fairness in baseline treatment: they retrain DiT with augmentation to strengthen it, ablate ELBO weighting schemes, and even compare against few-step diffusion (MeanFlow) to preempt efficiency objections. Detailed training settings in the appendix support reproducibility, and code/models are stated to be released.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: the main contribution is applying existing any-order AR machinery (RandAR) to classification with a Monte Carlo lower bound, which is a fairly straightforward combination; the value rests primarily on the empirical analysis and findings rather than a new algorithm.

In-domain accuracy still trails DINOv2 (0.813 vs 0.827 for XL), so the claim of 'competitive' with SSL discriminative models is only partially supported and mostly holds on OOD sets; the paper is appropriately careful here but the advantage is not decisive.

Some evaluations use 2K-image subsets of IN-Val/IN-S/IN-C due to compute cost of 1000-class likelihood evaluation; no error bars or significance tests are reported, so some differences (e.g., RandAR vs DINOv2 on IN-C JPEG) are within plausible noise.

A confound remains in the raster vs random-order comparison: the random-order RandAR model is a weaker generative model per single order (as the authors note), so it is not fully disentangled whether gains come purely from order marginalization versus other interactions of pretraining objective and classifier behavior.

Computational cost of generative classification still scales with the number of classes (M classes x K orders forward passes), which limits practicality at large label spaces; the paper acknowledges this but only as future work (distillation).

The hypothesis for why the lower-bound estimator outperforms direct likelihood (alignment with the training objective) is plausible but not conclusively verified; similarly, explanations for prefix-length behavior remain speculative.
No explicit broader societal impact or limitations section in the main text beyond the computational-cost remark in the conclusion.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: the paper identifies a concrete, previously underexplored limitation of AR-based generative classifiers (fixed token order inducing restrictive inductive bias) and provides a principled remedy via order marginalization, with a formal lower bound derived via Jensen's inequality.

Strong empirical support: comprehensive comparisons across discriminative (ViT, DINOv2), joint (DAT), diffusion (DiT, SiT with fair weighting ablations), and AR baselines at matched architecture/resolution/token count, at two model scales (L/16, XL/16), with careful reproduction of baselines lacking public checkpoints.

The order-marginalized RandAR classifier achieves state-of-the-art among generative classifiers and, notably, competes with DINOv2 on several OOD benchmarks (IN-R, IN-S, IN-C Gaussian) — a first for GCs — while being up to ~25x faster than diffusion classifiers.

Unusually thorough analysis and ablations: per-token likelihood and accuracy analyses (Figs. 3-5), tokenizer robustness study (MaskGIT vs LlamaGen with noise-augmentation fix), likelihood-estimation strategy ablation (Table 5), masked-diffusion equivalence derivation (Appendix D) with empirical AR-vs-MD comparison, generalization to RAR (Sec. 6.6), few-step diffusion comparison (MeanFlow), WILDS real-world shift evaluation, and qualitative error analysis vs DINOv2.

Good methodological hygiene: shared sampled orders across classes, fair ELBO weighting ablations for DM baselines, subset-size validation, code/models promised, and extensive appendix details supporting reproducibility.
Honest framing of trade-offs: acknowledges in-domain accuracy gap to DINOv2 (-1.4% for XL), extra cost of K>1, and computes cost as a key GC limitation in the conclusion.
weaknesses: The claimed efficiency advantage (up to 25x) is measured against 250-step diffusion classifiers; the comparison to fewer-step or faster likelihood-estimation alternatives is only partially addressed (MeanFlow performs poorly, but the efficiency claim is heavily setup-dependent), so headline numbers should be read cautiously.

Despite strong relative results, absolute in-domain accuracy still trails DINOv2, and evaluation on 2K subsets of IN-Val/IN-S/IN-C (to keep the 1000-class likelihood computation tractable) introduces some sampling uncertainty, though the authors report subset-size checks.

The theoretical story has a gap: the Jensen lower bound on the order-marginalized likelihood outperforms the direct Monte Carlo estimate of the true likelihood, explained only by an informal hypothesis about training-objective alignment; a deeper theoretical or empirical justification would strengthen the contribution.

Findings rest primarily on one any-order architecture (RandAR); the RAR experiment is a helpful but limited generalization check, and results on non-image-centric datasets (ObjectNet, COCO) show DINOv2 still clearly ahead, limiting the practical case for GCs in those settings.

Computational demands remain substantial (K forward passes per class across 1000 classes), so practical adoption is questionable; this is acknowledged but the reviewer would have welcomed a stronger discussion of deployment scenarios.
No explicit societal-impact or broader-limitation statement in the main text beyond computational cost.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core insight: the paper identifies token ordering as an important, previously overlooked inductive bias in AR-based generative classifiers, supported by an intuitive motivating example (Fig. 1) and systematic analysis (Figs. 3-5).

Simple, principled method: order-marginalized likelihood estimation via the Jensen lower bound (Eq. 5) is elegant, easy to implement on top of existing any-order AR models (RandAR), and theoretically connected to masked-diffusion ELBOs (Appendix D), which the authors exploit for an interesting AR-vs-MD evaluation comparison.

Strong and comprehensive empirical evidence: the method consistently outperforms diffusion classifiers (DiT, SiT, REPA variants, MeanFlow), prior AR classifiers (LlamaGen, VAR, A-VARC+), and joint models (DAT) at matched model size, resolution, and token count; efficiency analysis (Fig. 6) shows up to 25x faster inference than DiT.

First meaningful comparison of generative classifiers against a modern SSL baseline (DINOv2), with a nuanced result: the GC trails slightly in-domain but surpasses DINOv2 on most OOD benchmarks — a notable milestone for generative classifiers.

Good breadth of validation: ablations over K, likelihood estimation strategy, tokenizers (MaskGIT vs LlamaGen, with a sensible noise-augmentation fix), generalization to RAR (Table 6), WILDS real-world shifts (Table 7), non-image-centric datasets (ObjectNet, COCO), and informative error analysis (Fig. 7).
Reproducibility is well supported: detailed training settings (Appendix A), released code/models, and public checkpoints or faithful reproductions for all baselines.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is relatively simple — averaging order-conditional log-likelihoods with a shared set of K sampled permutations is a straightforward application of Jensen's inequality to an existing any-order AR model; the paper's value rests primarily on the insight and empirical study rather than algorithmic novelty.

Results are tied to a single backbone family (RandAR); the RAR generalization check (Table 6) uses a retrained variant without order annealing rather than a strong native any-order model, so the breadth of the conclusion across architectures is somewhat limited.

Classification still requires K forward passes per class token, so full 1000-class evaluation remains computationally heavy; the authors evaluate on 2K-image subsets for large benchmarks, and per-token accuracy (~0.2) shows individual token predictions are weak, with performance driven largely by aggregation over many tokens and orders.

The DINOv2 comparison uses models retrained by the authors on ImageNet1K (200 epochs), whereas DINOv2 in its full form is trained on much larger data; the 'competes with DINOv2' claim should be interpreted carefully, and there remains a ~1.4% in-domain accuracy gap.

Several mechanistic explanations (e.g., why the lower bound outperforms the direct Monte Carlo estimate, why prefix ~70-80 tokens are most discriminative) are hypotheses rather than established findings, though they are candidly labeled as such.
No explicit societal-impact discussion, though the limitations of GC compute cost are honestly acknowledged in the conclusion.
